newsitem.title: USA: U.S.-EU sparring over Boeing a harbinger of future.
newsitem.headline: U.S.-EU sparring over Boeing a harbinger of future.

text.p: The transatlantic battle over the merger of Boeing Co. and McDonnell Douglas Corp. that nearly ignited a trade war could be a harbinger of things to come as the world economy becomes more interdependent and global competition intensifies.

Boeing and McDonnell Douglas, two American aerospace companies whose $16 billion merger had been cleared in the United States, found the deal under attack in Europe. The European Union reviewed and initially withheld approval of the deal because the companies sell there in competition with the European consortium, Airbus Industrie.
The head of the U.S. agency that cleared the merger, Robert Pitofsky, of the Federal Trade Commission, predicted foreign scrutiny of mergers will be common in the future.

"More and more of those reviews are going to take place as global competition explodes," he told a Senate committee. "My view is that if a transaction has an effect on the consumers of a particular country, then that country has a right to review that under its system of law, its competition system."
World trade has multiplied tenfold in the past 20 years, he said, often making transactions subject to review by multiple countries.
Despite the many mergers affecting companies in Europe and the United States, no international standards govern their review and none are being developed.

After the wrenching Boeing debate, which involved President Bill Clinton, his cabinet and the Congress -- along with European leaders -- and threatened a trade war, the Europeans are ready to take another look. But Americans are not.
Sir Leon Brittan, who heads the European Union's trade unit, said in a statement following the Boeing decision that negotiations should begin for broadly based standards.
"I have long believed that we need an international agreement on competition rules," he said. "Otherwise there are bound to be more clashes."
Brittan said that he and Competition Commissioner Karel Van Miert want to expand a World Trade Organization working group on antitrust, organized at last year's WTO meeting.
But the United States goverment is wary at best, although some in the private sector -- including Boeing -- are enthusiastic about the idea.
At one end of the spectrum are members of Congress, who resist the idea that any other country should review mergers of American-based companies.

"McDonnell Douglas and Boeing have come together in an honest merger that has been OK in America," said Washington state Republican Linda Smith in one typical comment during debate last week. "We should not have another country come in and tell us to do something different."

Members of Congress insisted the Federal Trade Commission, which gave Boeing a green light, was the only legitimate forum for review. Boeing itself -- with customers from Cameroon to China and France to the Philippines -- believes international rules are a good idea.

"In a global economy I think a single set of rules ... as opposed to multiple jurisdictions ... is in fact preferable" to handle mergers, Boeing CEO Phil Condit told reporters after the EU decision last week. "Over time (business and government have) got to keep working in that direction."
But the United States is not ready for a broad international agreement.
Assistant Attorney General Joel Klein, who heads the antitrust division, helped establish the WTO group last year.
Klein has always drawn a firm line against a comprehensive international plan, preferring bilateral agreements. Some in government fear an international agreement would impinge on U.S. sovereignty.
The United States and the EU are putting the finishing touches on a "positive comity" pact that spells out when each side may ask the other to investigate antitrust violations.
The most far-reaching pact was recently signed with Australia. It permits the exchange of confidential evidence -- such as grand jury testimony -- needed to catch companies that fix prices.
But Princeton University professor Robert Willig, a former Justice Department official, is unimpressed.
Willig says the Australian pact is "merely an agreement for process," noting it "explicitly mentions that co-operation would proceed without any implication of endorsement of each other's outcomes."
